description:
Team Halmahera is a small AI team from Jakarta, Indonesia. We built Orbitalis for Dancing with the SARs: it turns NISAR radar into inspection leads for groundwater regulators. Our team covers product and business, product design and front-end engineering, research and model evaluation, AI and backend engineering, and data engineering. Past results: 1st place at LIDM 2024, and 3rd place at Gemastik 2024 and the Meta Llama Hackathon 2024. Website: halmahera.site

Dancing in the moonlight.
summary: Orbitalis turns NISAR radar into inspection leads for the people who manage groundwater in Jakarta. Parts of Jakarta sink more than 10 cm a year, mostly because deep wells pump out groundwater. Jakarta banned groundwater use in large zones in 2023, but regulators cannot see where pumping goes on. Orbitalis reads NISAR L-band interferograms (GUNW) over all of mainland Jakarta from two directions, stacks sixteen pairs from June to October 2026, and finds places that sink faster than the ground around them: the bowl shape a hidden pump leaves. The web app shows these bowls on a 3D map with a triage queue, opens a digital twin of the ground under each one, and lets a regulator schedule and record field visits. A 480 m grid shows the measured sinking and the WorldPop population, and any cell can be flagged as a new lead. Every number comes from NISAR or WorldPop, with its source. A lead is a reason to inspect, never proof. With NISAR's 12-day repeat, the same pipeline can check after every pass whether enforcement, pipes, and recharge slow the sinking.
details:
The Orbitalis sinking grid: the NISAR sinking rate of every 480 m cell across Jakarta, from slow (green) to fast (orange).

What it does

Orbitalis helps groundwater regulators find where heavy groundwater extraction is likely happening in Jakarta, decide which cases to handle first, and check whether groundwater is recovering. Satellite radar measurements of ground sinking are turned into a ranked queue of pumping leads.

  • Prioritize: regulators rank leads by severity (signal strength and sinking rate) and by impact (number of people nearby).
  • 3D digital twin: each lead opens a model of the ground, showing soil layers, buildings, and a year timeline to 2050 if the measured rate continues.
  • Act: a regulator can schedule a visit, assign an inspector, and record the outcome.
  • Verify: after action is taken, the same radar record shows whether sinking slows or the ground rebounds, as evidence that the groundwater program is working.
  • Explore: users can switch the map between four layers (leads, sinking, people, radar passes), open any 480 m cell, and flag it as a new lead.

The 3D digital twin of the Kalideres bowl in street view: the buildings above the sinking ground, and the ground in 2035 at the measured NISAR rate.

How it works

The science: InSAR

The app uses InSAR (interferometric SAR). A radar satellite measures the phase of the signal reflected from the ground, which depends on the distance between satellite and ground. When two images of the same area are taken at different times and compared, any ground movement shows up as a phase difference, producing a map of displacement called an interferogram. NISAR collects this in L-band (23.8 cm wavelength), which gives better subsidence estimates in vegetated areas than shorter wavelengths.

The data pipeline

  1. Find the data. A Python job searches ASF for NISAR L2 GUNW products over Jakarta: track 10 ascending and track 18 descending (frame 92), 8 consecutive pairs each.
  2. Read only what is needed. The job reads only the mainland Jakarta window (about 33 x 33 km, 80 m grid) with HTTP range requests, so one pair takes about 1.7 MB instead of 2.3 GB.
  3. Clean each pair. It masks water and pixels with coherence below 0.6, removes the ionosphere phase screen, and converts phase to millimeters of range change (ground moving toward or away from the satellite).
  4. Stack per track. It removes the regional ramp, stacks the pairs, and divides by the time.
  5. Combine two directions. The two tracks look from the east and from the west, so the job solves for vertical and east motion. In the vertical rate, a negative value means the ground is sinking (land subsidence), and a positive value means the ground is rising, which can indicate groundwater uplift or recovery.
  6. Find subsidence bowls. A bowl is a local depression that forms when the ground compacts over a heavily pumped aquifer. The job looks for a local peak at least 2.5 times the noise floor and 1.5 times its own uncertainty.
  7. Add people. It averages the rate into 480 m cells and adds WorldPop 2026 population.
  8. Serve the app. The web app (Next.js on Cloudflare Workers) reads the job output as small JSON files. Scores are fixed formulas with visible weights. There is no machine learning model.

First results from real NISAR data

  • Coverage: 62% of the pixels have at least five usable pairs on both tracks.
  • Noise floor: the vertical noise floor is 15 mm/yr.
  • Known hotspots: the areas that published studies name as the fastest sinking (Muara Baru, Pluit, Penjaringan) show positive extra sinking.
  • Three bowls pass every test. The strongest is about 190 m in radius in Penjaringan: it sinks 82 +/- 39 mm/yr faster than the ground around it, at 5.3 times the noise floor. The others are in Kalideres (65 +/- 41 mm/yr) and at Rawakalong (55 +/- 35 mm/yr). Both tracks see all three.

A bowl is a reason for a field visit, not proof of a pump.

Benefits

  • Helps policymakers see which areas are affected by groundwater extraction.
  • Prioritizes places with a large population or a large economy.

The public landing page explains why Jakarta sinks and who can use the radar measurements.

Known limits

  • The NISAR rate is relative to the ground within about 3 km, not an absolute rate.
  • It is a simple stack, not a full time series (MintPy is planned).
  • Each bowl rate is only 1.5 to 2 times its uncertainty, because there are only 3.5 months of data.
  • The projection to 2050 is the measured rate times the years, not a forecast.

Tools

  • Web: TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, MapLibre GL, three.js with React Three Fiber, Tailwind CSS 4, shadcn/ui, Better Auth, Drizzle ORM, PostgreSQL (Neon), Cloudflare Workers, Bun, Turborepo.
  • Data jobs: Python 3.11, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj, Pillow.
  • Basemap: OpenStreetMap data through CARTO.
  • Use of AI: we used Claude Code (Anthropic) to write and review parts of the code and to draft this text. The team reviewed and tested the output. No AI model runs inside the product.
